selectedMoves.claimSummary: Religion's growth amid danger and modern disruption is explained by demand for certainty and consolation, not by the truth or superiority of its explanations.
selectedMoves.reasonSummary: Hitchens links insecurity to human consolation-seeking, argues religion still recycles discredited myths, and contrasts those with philosophy, aesthetics, science, and reason.

inferenceSummary.premise: People predictably seek stable consolation under risk, while religious popularity has not produced improved explanations.
inferenceSummary.inference: Psychological demand explains growth without validating the content that satisfies it.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Religious resurgence is not evidence that God exists or is great.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a human explanation for persistent belief and alternative sources of consolation and understanding.

selectedMoves.importanceRationale: It addresses popularity and existential usefulness, important but secondary evidence for the motion.

responseComponents.description: Explains felt need and persistence through insecurity and consolation rather than divine contact.

selectedMoves.attributionRationale: The constitutional objection to state chaplains and praise of reason identify Hitchens, but captions lack labels.
selectedMoves.materialWordingRationale: The insecurity and false-consolation thesis is clear, though several images and transitions are poorly recognized.
selectedMoves.spanLengthRationale: The psychological explanation and comparison with secular consolations must remain together to establish both cause and alternative.

sourceSpan.excerpt: do not believe that everyone believes in things that are illogical I think that and there are different theologians that approach it differently I guess the closest well not exactly where I am but Paul Tillich that talks about a personal God would be going in the direction that I believe I believe in my own experiences and my own relationship with God and that is not based on any illogical unbelievable act I do not believe things that are necessarily part of dogma and I think that Richard you whoever has the right to disbelieve it without being a freak but I don't think that I am a freak that believes in illogical things because I believe that the reason the world operates in a certain order is because there is a supreme force that ordered it and I don't think that I happen to agree with Richard that I think religion has been one of the most misused things in history but I don't think that has anything to do with the existence or non-existence of God I think that has something to do with man's misuse or use of what is is absolutely there and that is the Supreme Being thank you we have a

quoteEligibleExactSpans: a supreme force that ordered it
relatedEarlierMoves.claimSummary: Personal theism is neither illogical dogma nor institutional abuse because it rests on experience and the ordered operation of the world.
relatedEarlierMoves.reasonSummary: Sharpton invokes his own relationship with God and the inference from regular order to a supreme ordering force while agreeing that religion has often been misused.

inferenceSummary.premise: Personal experience and persistent natural order remain even after dogmatic and institutional claims are set aside.
inferenceSummary.inference: Those independent grounds can support a personal God without accepting every religious assertion.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Misused religion does not make Sharpton's personal belief illogical or false.

burdenContact.rationale: This integrates Sharpton's experiential and design grounds into his narrower affirmative position.

relatedEarlierMoves.importanceRationale: It is a concise later restatement of the exact version of theism the pro side asks to have assessed.

responseComponents.description: Returns to world order as a rational ground rather than relying on scientists' authority.
Maintains that his own experience supports relationship with God even if others interpret transcendence differently.

relatedEarlierMoves.attributionRationale: The personal-God defense and agreement about misuse identify Sharpton's reply; the source is unlabeled.
relatedEarlierMoves.materialWordingRationale: The experience, order, and misuse distinctions are repeated plainly with modest ASR noise.
